text-gray-700">Print</span></a></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div><div class="mt-8 md:mt-0 md:w-[300px] md:ml-8 shrink-0 print:!hidden hidden md:block"></div></div></section><section class="w-full px-5 xl:px-[72px] mx-auto max-w-[1440px] mb-8"><div class="relative flex flex-col md:flex-row"><div class="lg:w-[200px] lg:mr-6 shrink-0 print:!hidden"></div><div class="flex-grow min-w-0"><div class="lg:border-l border-gray-200 lg:pl-8"><div><div class="wysiwyg group is-wysiwyg"><div class="relative !mb-0"><div id="hygromas" class="absolute z-[-1]" style="top:-100px"></div></div><h2>Hygromas</h2><p>Hygromas are soft, benign, fluid-filled masses that form over bony prominences in young adult large- and giant-breed dogs in response to repetitive pressure or blunt trauma.<sup>1-3</sup> Hygromas are typically located over the elbows, although they have been reported in other regions (eg, tuber calcaneous, tuber ischium, carpus; <b>Figures 1</b> and <b>2</b>).<sup>1</sup> As the bony prominence hits the floor or other hard surfaces, subcutaneous tissue over the bone is damaged. Repetitive trauma results in formation of a pocket of serous fluid that is surrounded by a fibrous capsule and, in some cases, contains granulation tissue.<sup>1-3</sup></p><div class="exclude-wysiwyg"><div id="6JIopgAytq21F17l7ARUtz" class="!m-0"></div><div class="flex flex-col relative bg-gray-200"><img alt="A hygroma on a dog’s left lateral elbow." loading="lazy" text-gray-500 mt-4 ImageCaption_plain-text-label__mkWEA"><span class="font-bold pr-1">FIGURE 2</span><p>Ulcerated hygroma on the tarsus of a dog with a plantigrade stance secondary to neuropathy</p></div></div><p>Most hygromas are nonpainful, but they can enlarge, ulcerate, and become infected (<b>Figures 2</b> and <b>3</b>).<sup>1-4</sup>  Prevention of hygroma formation and treatment for small, nonpainful hygromas involves elimination of blunt trauma to bony prominences by providing appropriate bedding or applying regional padding or coaptation devices (eg, casts, splints, bandages).<sup>1,4,5</sup> Large, ulcerated, or infected hygromas may require culture, drainage, open wound management, or surgical resection and reconstruction.<sup>1-3,6</sup> Even after aggressive treatment, pressure-relieving measures must be continued to allow the site to heal and to prevent future recurrences.<sup>3</sup></p><div class="exclude-wysiwyg"><div absolute shadow-darker rounded-full"><svg width="28" height="28" fill="none" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class=""><rect width="28" height="28" rx="14" fill="#FFFFFF"></rect><path d="M19.5 11.5v-3h-3.001M11.5 8.5h-3v3M19.5 16.5v3h-3.001M11.5 19.5h-3v-3" stroke="#0A2447" stroke-width="2.1" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"></path></svg></button></div><div class="text-xsm text-gray-500 mt-4 ImageCaption_plain-text-label__mkWEA"><span class="font-bold pr-1">FIGURE 3</span><p>Chronic ulcerated elbow hygroma</p></div></div><p>When selecting or manufacturing a coaptation device, fit is the most important consideration. An ill-fitted coaptation device can result in discomfort, swelling, dermatitis, local tissue necrosis, ulcerations, and muscle atrophy from immobility. In addition, if appropriate positioning is not maintained, the device may not protect the area adequately from further trauma. The device should be lightweight and inexpensive, distribute pressure away from bony prominences, allow unimpeded motion and mobility, and permit appropriate blood flow to the region.<sup>4,7</sup> Doughnut-style padding can be helpful for prevention of hygroma formation or enlargement (<b>Figure 4</b>). However, in dogs with ulcerations (<b>Figure 5</b>) or surgical reconstructions, doughnut-style padding redistributes pressure circumferentially to all surrounding tissues, inhibiting blood flow and healing.<sup>4</sup> Application of padding distal to the hygroma (<b>Figure 6</b>) can prevent contact of the region with hard surfaces while allowing joint movement and maintaining blood flow along the proximal half of the area. A homemade system from readily available products is especially useful when owner travel is restricted.</p><div class="exclude-wysiwyg"><div id="1Haf3PqZB7yzvAs5ndRFHc" class="!m-0"></div><div pool noodle for large limb</p></li></ul><div class="exclude-wysiwyg"><div id="QFQw3Wz69ZflWBencOZVW" class="!m-0"></div><div class="flex flex-col relative bg-gray-200"><img alt="Supplies for bandaging 1</h3><p>Starting from a point 1 inch below (ie, distal to) the olecranon, or the lowest point of the hygroma, measure the distance to the carpal pad.</p><div class="exclude-wysiwyg"><div 2</h3><p>Mark a pool noodle with the measurement from Step 1. Cut it to the appropriate length, then use scissors or a box cutter to split it down the center of one side lengthwise.</p><div class="exclude-wysiwyg"><div id="5bhGLfNaGtdQ9ecr0eWhtn" class="!m-0"></div><div class="flex flex-col relative bg-gray-200"><img alt="A section of a pool noodle has been cut lengthwise." loading="lazy" width="315" height="475" decoding="async" data-nimg="1" class="object-contain max-h-[calc(80vh-140px)] h-auto w-full" style="color:transparent;background-size:cover;background-position:50% 50%;background-repeat:no-repeat;background-image:url(&quot;data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg xmlns=&#x27;http://www.w3.org/2000/svg&#x27; Provide the pet owner with extra stockinette so soiled pieces can be laundered.</p><div class="exclude-wysiwyg"><div id="5mb2l3oDG59zJb4csVM8rF" class="!m-0"></div><div class="flex flex-col relative bg-gray-200"><img alt="Stockingette bandage material is held up to a dog’s leg. Pull down the excess cuff of stockinette over the proximal and distal edges of the pool noodle, then secure the noodle and stockinette in place with Velcro straps, Velcro tape, or adhesive elastic tape.</p><div class="exclude-wysiwyg"><div id="7Ih952URql3k2uucSCBtCW" class="!m-0"></div><div class="flex flex-col relative bg-gray-200"><img alt="A completed coaptation device on a recumbent dog’s https://images.ctfassets.net/4dmg3l1sxd6g/ypL7mxMrqLSguIUCYjvvS/dc52a419528bd405e3247b9b2dd48799/ProP_Bandages-Step-4B.jpg_-_en?fm=webp&amp;w=1200&amp;q=75 1920w, https://images.ctfassets.net/4dmg3l1sxd6g/ypL7mxMrqLSguIUCYjvvS/dc52a419528bd405e3247b9b2dd48799/ProP_Bandages-Step-4B.jpg_-_en?fm=webp&amp;w=1200&amp;q=75 2048w, https://images.ctfassets.net/4dmg3l1sxd6g/ypL7mxMrqLSguIUCYjvvS/dc52a419528bd405e3247b9b2dd48799/ProP_Bandages-Step-4B.jpg_-_en?fm=webp&amp;w=1200&amp;q=75 3840w" src="https://images.ctfassets.net/4dmg3l1sxd6g/ypL7mxMrqLSguIUCYjvvS/dc52a419528bd405e3247b9b2dd48799/ProP_Bandages-Step-4B.jpg_-_en?fm=webp&amp;w=1200&amp;q=75"/></div></div><p><b>Author Insights</b></p><p>The pool noodle elevates the limb off the floor to prevent abrupt or traumatic compression along the pressure point. Because the noodle is placed only along one side of the region experiencing pressure, it does not apply 360-degree compression of the tissues as a doughnut bandage would and therefore does not obstruct blood flow all the way around the affected area.</p><p>If the Velcro straps or tape cause pressure on the cranial or dorsal aspect of the limb, especially if the limb is large, add a piece of foam to fill the gap between the split sides of the noodle to prevent pressure sores or irritation.</p><hr/><h3>Step 5</h3><p>Assess the fit of the device by watching the dog walk and checking for any pressure points.</p><div class="exclude-wysiwyg"><div id="24Xru4nuoPQ70hPgvflXjQ" class="!m-0"></div><div class="flex flex-col relative bg-gray-200"><img alt="A standing dog has coaptation devices on both front limbs. width=&#x27;100%25&#x27; height=&#x27;100%25&#x27;/%3E%3CfeComposite operator=&#x27;out&#x27; in=&#x27;s&#x27;/%3E%3CfeComposite in2=&#x27;SourceGraphic&#x27;/%3E%3CfeGaussianBlur
